$comment: SPEC §3.4's pronunciation-override system, seeded. Per-locale term → the spelling a TTS engine says correctly. §3.4 permits 'grapheme→phoneme OR vendor-native lexicon format'; this is the former, because a vendor-hosted lexicon is a resource that has to be created through the vendor's API and would make the dictionary un-reviewable from the admin surface §3.4 requires.
$scope: NOT §3.4's full corpus. That is 200 astrology terms, 150 given names, 100 surnames, 80 cities, 60 festivals — authored by the localisation lead and signed off by the Jyotish lead, per §3.4's own ownership. These are the tradition terms M9's live run touched plus the day-division vocabulary a call will reach first. Every row is `status: draft` for exactly that reason: nothing here has been through §3.4's native panel, and a row that claimed otherwise would be the review being skipped rather than pending.
$why_these: Cartesia Ink transcribed spoken 'rahu kaal' as the single token 'Rahukaal' (M9 live run, 13 Aug 2026). That is a compound-word join, not a mishearing, and it pointed at the same seam on the TTS side: a term the engine treats as one token is a term it stresses as one word. The claim lexicon's half of this is fixed separately (CL-015, `_separator_variants`); this is the spoken half.
$review: §3.4: 'Every override records author + review status.' `reviewed_by` is null on every row below because nobody has reviewed them. The §14 native reviewer owns that, and `status` stays `draft` until they do.

hi.$register: aap-register, Devanagari. §3.3: 'Devanagari input to TTS always' for Hindi.

terms.note: Two words, and the space is load-bearing — joined it becomes RAA-hu-kaal with one stress instead of two. The double space is a pause hint, not a typo.
The joined spelling users and STT both produce; spoken the same as the spaced one.

hi-Latn.$register: Hinglish, Latin script (§2.4). The respelling targets an engine reading Latin text with Hindi intonation (§3.3's tts language `hi`).

terms.note: Doubling the first vowel stops the clipped 'RA-hu'; the gap keeps two stresses.
What Ink returns for spoken 'rahu kaal'. Same sound, one token.
Listed with no change so the review surface shows it was considered, not missed.

en.$register: Warm Indian-neutral (§3.3). English readers mangle these hardest — an engine reading 'rahu kaal' as English gives 'RAY-hoo KAYL'.
